1 Motivation
Kafka Connect sink tasks currently consume through ordinary consumer groups. Kafka partitions are assigned exclusively to task consumers, which limits useful input parallelism to the partition count.
Share groups allow different tasks to acquire different records from the same partition. This is useful for independent, unordered work delivered to databases, services, or other external systems.
However, changing the consumer implementation is insufficient.
Existing sink connectors may depend on:
Exclusive ownership of a source partition.
Ordered delivery.
Partition lifecycle callbacks.
Offset-based recovery.
Buffered writes that become durable only duringflush()orpreCommit().
In particular, ordinarySinkTask.put()is allowed to return before destination writes are durable.put returns after buffering -> worker ACCEPTs input -> worker crashes -> buffered destination write is lost
Share mode therefore needs an explicit connector-completion contract.
This proposal introduces an opt-in share sink runtime for compatible connectors. It providesat-least-once delivery by acknowledging exact acquired inputs only after their destination outcomes are durable.
Destination effects can repeat when a write succeeds but acknowledgement does not complete.
Note:
Share Groups (KIP-932) introduce queue semantics for Kafka consumers. Unlike consumer groups, Share Groups do not assign partitions exclusively.
Instead, records from a partition areacquiredby any available consumer in the group. After processing, the consumeracknowledgesthe record (ACCEPT, RELEASE, ARCHIEVED, or REJECT).
This provides:
-Elastic Scaling:Decouples parallelism from partition count,
-No Head-of-Line Blocking:Supportsunordered message processing; if a task slows down, records time out and are redelivered to available workers.
-Seamless Scaling:Eliminates "rebalance storms" by removing the partition assignment protocol, ensuring zero downtime during task membership changes.
Note: The share groups are only suitable for connectors withidempotent, order-independentprocessing.
3. Public Interfaces
poll -> conversion / SMT -> put -> later preCommit / flush -> offset commit
| User-visible behaviour | Ordinary sink mode | Share sink mode
| Selection | Default, orconsumer.type=consumer | consumer.type=share
| Distribution | One task owns each assigned partition | Several tasks can process distinct records from one partition
| Progress tracking | Committed partition offsets | Individual record acknowledgements
| Successfulput() | May buffer writes for later flush | Every supplied record must already be durable
| Slow processing | Task must remain within consumer polling limits | Owner thread renews record leases within processing limits
| Recovery | Records after committed offsets can return | Records without confirmed completion can return
| Ordering | Partition dispatch order; destination behaviour depends on |
Concurrent and out-of-order completion
Rest API :
Duplicates remain possible and will be taken care in next enhancement with txn. Mostly using KIP-1289:1. Worker A durably writes record 100 to the database.
2. Worker A crashes before Kafka confirms its ACCEPT.
3. The acquisition expires and Worker B receives record 100.
4. Worker B writes it again.
Share-compatible task contract
Introduce a public opt-in task type:public abstract class ShareSinkTask extends SinkTask {
}
Its contract differs from ordinarySinkTask:
A successfulput(records)return means every supplied record has a durable destination outcome.
Failures must be reported.
Partial destination success before failure remains possible.
The implementation supports sparse, unordered inputs and nonexclusive source partitions.
Offset frontiers do not determine share acknowledgement eligibility.
Existing sink connectors continue using their current contract in ordinary consumer mode.
